planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed well past last frost in hot, dry, full-sun conditions; Khatouni is a traditional Khorasan Province landrace melon and sets its best sugars under the long, hot, arid summers typical of eastern Iran.

directions: Khatouni is a traditional Iranian melon landrace long grown around Khorasan Province in northeastern Iran, where it is prized as one of the sweetest and most aromatic of the many named Persian melon types. Fruits are oval to oblong with pale, finely ribbed or faintly netted rind that ripens from green to creamy yellow-gold, enclosing thick, crisp, pale green-white flesh with an intense floral sweetness and almost no musky aroma compared to Western cantaloupes. Grow it on raised, well-drained beds in full sun with steady but not excessive irrigation, since Khatouni was selected under arid, furrow-irrigated desert-oasis conditions and is prone to splitting or diluted flavor with overwatering. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine and the rind color has fully turned, and expect a long, hot growing season of three months or more for full flavor development.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds
Seed Savers Exchange
University of California Cooperative Extension, Cucurbit Crops

planting.note: Plant rooted suckers or cuttings in spring in lean, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; this seedless cultivar is propagated vegetatively rather than from seed and is the commercial source of nearly all dried zereshk sold internationally.

directions: Zereshk-e Bidaneh is the named seedless barberry cultivar grown commercially in the high desert orchards of Qaenat and other districts of South Khorasan Province, Iran, which together produce the great majority of the world's dried zereshk sold for zereshk polo (barberry rice pilaf) and other Persian dishes. Unlike the common European barberry, this cultivar sets small, oblong, bright-red berries that are naturally seedless or nearly so, allowing them to be dried whole without the gritty seeds found in wild barberry fruit. Plant in lean, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun; established bushes tolerate the cold winters and hot, dry summers of the Iranian plateau and need only modest irrigation once rooted. Berries are hand- or mechanically harvested in autumn and traditionally sun- or shade-dried on rooftops before the tart, cranberry-like fruit is cleaned and packaged.
sources: Iranian Journal of Horticultural Science, barberry (Berberis spp.) cultivation studies
Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Iran barberry production reports
Iran Ministry of Agriculture-Jihad, South Khorasan barberry extension bulletins

planting.note: Plant offshoots or tissue-cultured palms in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Mazafati is a soft-date cultivar that needs long, intensely hot summers and low humidity at ripening to avoid fruit spoilage.

directions: Mazafati is a premier Iranian soft-date cultivar grown chiefly around Bam and Jiroft in Kerman Province, prized for its dark brown to near-black, thin-skinned fruit with exceptionally moist, soft, caramel-sweet flesh and a small, slender seed. It is one of the most widely exported Iranian date varieties, usually sold fresh-packed or lightly dried rather than fully sun-dried, since its high moisture content makes it unsuited to long dry-storage compared to drier Iranian cultivars. Give palms deep, fertile, well-drained soil, full sun, and regular irrigation through the long, hot growing season, along with the intense summer heat and low humidity that southeastern Iran provides and that Mazafati needs to ripen properly without fruit souring. Hand-pollinate female flower clusters if wild pollinators and male palms are not reliably present, and protect ripening bunches from rain and excess humidity, which can cause the soft fruit to ferment or mold.
sources: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, date palm cultivar reports (Iran)
Iranian Journal of Horticultural Science, Phoenix dactylifera cultivar studies
University of California Cooperative Extension, Date Production Manual

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Touriga Nacional is a naturally low-yielding variety and benefits from careful canopy and crop-load management to concentrate its intensely colored, aromatic fruit.

directions: Touriga Nacional is Portugal's most celebrated red wine grape, long grown in the Douro Valley and the Dão region, where it forms the backbone of premium vintage Port and increasingly of top-tier dry Douro and Dão red table wines. The small, thick-skinned, deeply pigmented berries give wines of intense color, firm tannin, and a distinctive aroma profile of violets, dark berries, and bay laurel, but the vine is naturally low-yielding, which led growers to favor more productive varieties until a quality-driven revival from the late twentieth century onward restored its reputation as Portugal's finest red grape. Train vines on a sturdy trellis in deep, well-drained, often schistous soil in full sun, and thin crop as needed, since restricting yield is essential to the variety's characteristic concentration. It ripens reliably in warm, long growing seasons and shows excellent drought tolerance once established, consistent with its origins in the hot, dry Douro terraces.
sources: Instituto dos Vinhos do Douro e do Porto
University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology
Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding & Jose Vouillamoz, 'Wine Grapes'

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis in deep, moisture-retentive clay soil in full sun; Baga is late-ripening and thick-skinned, traits that historically made it well suited to the humid, clay-rich Bairrada region of coastal Portugal.

directions: Baga is the dominant traditional red grape of the Bairrada region on Portugal's Atlantic coast, named for its small, tightly clustered, thick-skinned berries (baga means 'berry' in Portuguese). It produces deeply colored, high-acid, high-tannin wines that historically required long aging to soften and were also a traditional base for Bairrada's sparkling wines (espumante), made using the region's abundant limestone-clay soils and cooler, maritime-influenced climate. The variety buds early but ripens late, and its tight clusters and thick skins make it prone to botrytis bunch rot in wet autumns, so good canopy airflow and careful spray timing matter in humid sites. Grow on a sturdy trellis in deep, water-retentive clay-limestone soil in full sun, and expect a long hang time; modern winemakers increasingly pick slightly earlier and use softer extraction to tame Baga's famously assertive tannins while preserving its structure and aging potential.
sources: Comissão Vitivinícola da Bairrada
Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding & Jose Vouillamoz, 'Wine Grapes'
University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant seed tubers once soil has warmed past hard frost risk; Lumper is a late-maturing maincrop variety historically grown on marginal, poor ground and is highly susceptible to late blight, so good air circulation and blight-watch vigilance are essential.

directions: The Lumper is the Irish potato variety most closely associated with the Great Famine of the 1840s, when its heavy yields on poor land made it the dominant subsistence crop for Ireland's rural poor in the years before Phytophthora infestans devastated the country's potato crop. It produces irregular, knobby, pale-skinned tubers with floury white flesh, valued historically for productivity on marginal ground rather than culinary refinement, and it remains notably susceptible to late blight, a trait that contributed to the catastrophic crop failures of 1845-1849. Plant certified seed tubers in well-drained soil and hill rows as shoots emerge, watching closely for blight symptoms through the growing season since this variety carries little of the resistance bred into modern cultivars. Today it is maintained mainly by heritage seed savers and famine-history educational gardens rather than for mainstream production, and it offers a direct, living link to nineteenth-century Irish agricultural history.
sources: Irish Seed Savers Association
Teagasc
European Cultivated Potato Database

common_name: Skerry Blue Potato (Irish Heritage Blue-Skinned Potato)

planting.note: Plant seed tubers once soil has warmed past hard frost risk; Skerry Blue is a nineteenth-century Irish maincrop variety with distinctive blue-purple skin and was noted historically for somewhat better blight tolerance than the Lumper, though it is still far less resistant than modern cultivars.

directions: Skerry Blue is an Irish heritage potato dating to the mid-1800s, grown historically alongside and sometimes in place of the famine-vulnerable Lumper, and is now preserved mainly through heritage seed collections such as the Irish Seed Savers Association. It is identified by its distinctive blue-purple skin over white flesh, a round-to-oval tuber shape, and a waxy-to-floury texture that cooks well boiled or roasted. Plant certified seed tubers in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and hill rows as the plants grow, which both increases yield and protects developing tubers from sunlight and greening. Lift maincrop tubers in autumn once the foliage has died back, and cure briefly before storing in a cool, dark, frost-free space; as with all unimproved heirloom potatoes, monitor closely for late blight since this variety lacks modern disease resistance.
sources: Irish Seed Savers Association
European Cultivated Potato Database
Teagasc
